repository.description: Open-Source Software factory for Open Models

issue.body:
The heavy-suite lock is two locks. A tree at or past #1264 takes a flock on
`/tmp/codeaf-suite-<uid>.lockfile`. A tree behind #1264 takes the older
directory lock at `/tmp/codeaf-suite-<uid>.lock`. Neither mechanism can see the
other, so the flock's exclusivity is at present a CLAIM THE BOX DOES NOT HONOUR.

## Observed on the box, 2026-09-20T18:35:25Z

A heavy suite running while the flock reads free:

- pid 4029204, `bash ./scripts/one-suite.sh go test -timeout 15m -count=1
  -count=1 -p 1 ./cmd/codeaf ./internal/tui3`, cwd
  `/home/santosh/src/cw0918-adaptive-folders`, alive.
- pid 4029208, its `go test`, alive.
- That tree is at `991a83d384f5197e99471bb05b4ac8a4d3c1b07e`, behind #1264. Its
  `scripts/one-suite.sh:31` reads `lock="/tmp/codeaf-suite-$(id -u).lock"`, with
  the comment explaining that the lock is a directory because mkdir is atomic.
- `/tmp/codeaf-suite-1001.lock` exists, created 14:29, and its `pid` file
  contains `4029204`, the live process.
- At the same instant `flock -n /tmp/codeaf-suite-1001.lockfile -c true` returns
  0, free, `lsof` on that file returns no holder, and the file's contents are a
  stale line from an earlier run at 18:12:10Z.

That run is behaving CORRECTLY by its own rules. It holds a lock. It is simply
holding one that current readers do not read.

## The failure is symmetric, and only one direction has been hit

DIRECTION ONE, live tonight. A stale tree holds the directory lock. A current
reader checks only the flock, sees free, and starts a second heavy suite beside
it. This is the direction that has been costing us unattributable reds and
timing numbers taken under contention nobody recorded.

DIRECTION TWO, not yet hit and worse. A current tree holds the flock. A stale
tree's runner checks only the directory, sees no holder, and starts beside it.
Same collision, opposite parties, and here the party clobbered is the one that
did everything right.

Dual-checking on the READ side fixes direction one only. It stops a current
reader starting beside a stale holder. It does nothing to stop a stale runner
starting beside a current holder, because that runner will never be taught to
read the flock: being unaware of the flock is what makes it stale.

## Immediate remedy, for anything that reads the lock

Wait on the directory lock first and the flock second. Both, in that order. A
gate doing this today can see pid 4029204 and queues behind it correctly.

## Durable remedy, for the shared script, and the reason to prefer it

During the transition, the current `scripts/one-suite.sh` should take BOTH
locks: the flock as now, and the old directory lock as well. It costs a mkdir.

What it buys is that a current tree becomes VISIBLE TO EVERY STALE READER STILL
OUT THERE, without any stale tree being changed. The invisibility then runs in
one direction only, and that direction is the safe one: a stale runner sees a
current holder and waits. Direction two closes without touching anything that is
behind the head.

The transition ends when nothing running on the box is behind #1264. Until
somebody can assert that, dual-hold is what makes the flock's claim true rather
than merely declared.

## Consequences worth recording while this is open

- Any `suite_lock_held` field written by a flock-only reader is false on exactly
  the runs where it matters.
- A ceiling that lowers while a suite holds the lock has not been lowering for
  these runs.
- Timing numbers taken "under the lock" during the transition are upper bounds
  with an unknown floor, and should be quoted that way rather than discarded.

Raised as an issue and not a patch because it changes a shared script that other
trees run.

issue.body:
Three shapes of test in this repo are structurally incapable of catching the
defect sitting next to them. Each one looks like coverage, reads like a
contract, and stays green through the bug it appears to guard. All three were
found in one night's work on the question-presentation surfaces, each beside a
real defect, and in every case the test was doing exactly what its name
promised.

This is written as a review question, not a proposal for a lint rule. See the
last section for why.

## 1. A test that pins a string

It asserts what a surface SAYS, word for word, and never asks what the surface
DOES. The assertion and the defect never meet.

Example. `internal/tui3/place_tasks_test.go:45`
`TestTheTasksFootIsScreenOneEWordForWord` pins the tasks page footer exactly.
Three more pin the same foot: `:91`, `:129`, `:204`. All four pass while the
page answers landings with digit keys that the footer never names, which breaks
the page's own law that nothing bound goes unnamed.

What the replacement asserts: press every key the page binds and assert the
footer names it, and press the keys the footer names and assert they do
something. A string test is fine as a companion to that and is not a substitute
for it.

## 2. A test that compares two booleans

It asserts that two readings AGREE and never that either is RIGHT. Both sides
can be wrong together, and the test stays green while they are.

Example. `internal/session/attach_test.go:433`
`TestNeedsPersonAgreesWithPresence` walks the lanes and pins that the agent's
`NeedsPerson()` agrees with the presence file's boolean. It never asserts that
the accompanying reason is non-empty, so it passes for a lane that says a person
is needed and says nothing about what for. That is a mark a person cannot act
on, and it survived because the only test in the area compares two booleans to
each other.

What the replacement asserts: the CONTENT each side carries, not their
agreement. For this case, that every lane which sets the boolean also produces a
sentence, and that the sentence names that lane's own question.

## 3. A test that pins one side of a pair

Two readers describe the same state and only one of them is pinned. The unpinned
side drifts, and nothing goes red.

Example. A landed task whose acceptance is still merging is described by two
readers. The record card at `internal/session/question.go:2987` says the person
already answered. The line home at `internal/session/taskpresence.go:1004` still
says `your call`, because it reads `PendingDecisions`, which filters on node
state alone. The card side is pinned five times in
`internal/session/questionlifecycle_test.go`, at `:254`, `:297`, `:328`, `:354`
and `:405`. The home side is pinned zero times. Five to nothing.

What the replacement asserts: both readers of one state, in one test, agreeing
about that state. This shape is the most useful of the three because it is
COUNTABLE. Count the tests per side before believing a pair is covered.

## The same family outside tests

Two more instances of the same shape were seen the same day in tooling rather
than in tests: a formatting check whose command exits zero whether or not it
found anything, and a summary line that reports only the last command in a
chain, so an earlier failure is invisible. A check whose failure mode cannot
appear is worse than no check, because it spends the attention a real check
would have earned.

## Why this is not a lint rule

None of the three is reliably detectable from source. A rule that caught a third
of them would restart exactly the same false comfort one level up, which is the
disease rather than the cure.

The review question instead, to ask of any test that looks like coverage:

**What would have to be broken for this test to fail? If the answer does not
include the defect it sits next to, it is not covering that defect.**

Three follow-ups that catch most of it in practice:

1. Does it assert what a surface says, or what it does?
2. Does it assert that two things agree, or that either one is right?
3. If two readers describe one state, how many tests does each side have?

issue.title: tui3: a standing row stopped for permission says the line, not asks: it

repository.name: CodeAF
repository.description: Open-Source Software factory for Open Models

issue.body:
A watch that stopped because a call needed permission drew a row reading

```
asks: stopped: it needed your ok to run bash
```

Nobody asked anything. `standing.Item.NeedsPerson` carries two different things,
and its own doc says so: a QUESTION a firing put to a person in its own words,
or the line this build writes when a call was refused for want of somebody to
allow it. `switcherStandingNote` put the ask word over both.

The fix asks the one predicate that knows the difference,
`standing.IsPermissionLine`, and says the refusal bare, because it is already a
whole sentence about the item. The ask word stays for the other tenant.

This is the reading three siblings already take and this surface skipped:
`homepanel_needs.go` picks a different door word for a permission line,
`homestanding.go` picks a different destination, and
`standing.ClearNeedsPerson` will only clear the permission tenant. No second
list of spellings is added here; the spellings live in `standing`, in that one
predicate.

It also follows the precedent set a few lines above it in the same function:
`switcherConversationNote` already returns the consent gate's own sentence bare,
for the same reason and with a comment saying so.

## The test, and its failure on base

New: `TestAWatchStoppedForPermissionIsSaidNotAsked` in
`internal/tui3/switcher_test.go`, covering both tenants, so the word is proved
present for a question and absent for a refusal.

On base it fails with the defect in its own words:

```
switcher_test.go:124: the row puts the ask word over a line nobody asked:
got "asks: stopped: it needed your ok to run ..."
```

## The test that should have caught this and did not

There is none for this note in the permission state. The nearest test covers the
switcher's ranking and passes regardless of which tenant the line holds, because
it never reads the note's text in that state. Recorded here rather than left
implicit: this change adds the first assertion about what that row says when
nobody asked.

## Scope

One surface word. The mark, the glyph and the count are deliberately untouched:
whether a stopped-but-nothing-to-answer state should carry its own quieter mark,
and where its door goes, is a separate decision that has not been made. This
change does not prejudge it.

## Checks

`go test ./internal/tui3`, the whole package, ok in 340.670s, run on the base
the work was written against (`3d3b7542b`). This branch is that change
cherry-picked onto the current head (`952e0036a`), so the gate's run on this
head is the one that counts, and I am not quoting the earlier run as if it were
taken here.

issue.title: session: a sign-in and a harness ask say what they are waiting for

repository.name: CodeAF
repository.description: Open-Source Software factory for Open Models

issue.body:
Two lanes said a person was needed and said nothing about what for.

`personAskLanes` decides THAT a person is needed by OR-ing the lane books.
`waitingOnPerson` then takes the SENTENCE from `presenceAsk().Text`, which walks
the presence desk. Mark and sentence come from two different books, so a lane
counted in the OR that banks no desk row leaves `waiting: true, reason: ""`, and
a surface draws a mark nobody can act on.

Sign-in and the harness lane were both in that state. This routes them through
`presenceAskingWhole`, which is `raiseQuestion` plus the row, and returns one
closure that undoes both.

Three call sites, two conditions: `connect.go` for `connectAsks`, and
`harness.go` plus `harness_build.go`, which write the same `harnessAsks` book,
so the offer and the design card are one condition and one fix.

## What is deliberately NOT converted

Seven call sites raise through `raiseQuestion` and none of them banks a desk
row, so "banks a desk row" is the wrong criterion and would have converted all
seven. THE CRITERION IS WHETHER THE ROW ENDS UP WITH WORDS. One of the seven is
the door inside `presenceAskingWhole` itself and is not a lane. Of the remaining
six, three already get their words from another arm of `waitingOnPerson`: the
sub-harness offer, the fuel gate, and landings. Those three are untouched.

`task_landing_question.go` in particular is left alone: it drops its let-go
deliberately, because settle and answer own that question's retirement, and
banking a row there would leave nobody holding its remover.

## The failure is not always an empty sentence

When no lane has banked a row the reason is empty. When ANOTHER lane has one,
`presenceAsk()` returns that lane's words, so the row says a person is needed
and then describes a different question. Both cases are covered:
`TestWaitingSentenceConnectSignIn`, `TestWaitingSentenceHarnessAsk` and
`TestWaitingSentenceWrongOverlap`, the last being the wrong-sentence case rather
than the empty one.

## The test that should have caught this and did not

`TestNeedsPersonAgreesWithPresence` in `internal/session/attach_test.go` walks
the lanes and pins that `Agent.NeedsPerson()` agrees with the presence file's
boolean. It never asserts the reason is non-empty, so it passes for a lane that
says a person is needed and says nothing about what for. A test that compares
two booleans asserts that the two agree, never that either is right.

## Two comments, and who wrote them

The third commit is mine, not the change's author's. Both converted sites
carried a comment naming `question.go`'s `raiseQuestion` as the door, which
became false at those lines the moment they were converted. They now name
`presenceAskingWhole` and say what it adds. A doc comment that describes the
call above it incorrectly is worse than no comment, because the next reader
trusts it.

## Checks

The change was written against `3d3b7542b` and is cherry-picked here onto
`952e0036a`.

Stated plainly because it bears on how much this body is worth: THE CELL THAT
WROTE THIS DID NOT RUN THE DECLARED CHECK. Its report quotes
`go test ./internal/session -run TestPresenceAskReason` as passing, and no test
of that name exists in the package; a `-run` pattern matching nothing cannot
fail on behaviour. The whole-package check the work was briefed with was never
run. So the verification behind this branch is the diff, read line by line, plus
the gate on this head. Nothing here rests on the cell's own green.


## What would have objected

Naming it, because "the declared check was never run" says a hole existed and
not what closes it. The form that catches this is `run_tests` in `scripts/proof.sh`
on #1308, which runs the named tests and then checks that every name it asked
for actually RAN. Its own failing arm is in `internal/ci/prooflib_test.go`.

Against this branch it would have objected in the same second the step ran, and
it would have named the test that reported nothing. The point is not that
anything lied. `go test` reported its result faithfully: a filter matching
nothing is a run with nothing in it, and `ok` is the honest answer to that. What
the step could ever have caught was compilation and nothing else. A cell can
declare a check, run it, get a true green, and have proved that the package
builds.

Catching it the other way cost a diff read line by line, a name mismatch
noticed, and a grep to confirm.

issue.title: tui3: the front tab and the tab beside it agree about one conversation

repository.name: CodeAF
repository.description: Open-Source Software factory for Open Models

issue.body:
The front tab and the tab beside it answered the same question differently about
the same conversation.

A held tab's mark comes from `behindWatch.signal`, whose cached fact is fed by
`keeper.go`'s `needsPerson`, which calls the engine's `Agent.NeedsPerson`. So a
held tab counts every lane the engine counts.

The front tab's mark comes from `frontSignal`, which re-spells the lane list on
the surface. Two lanes the engine counts were missing from it: standing answers,
and landed tasks saying `your call`. So a conversation could carry the mark
while held and LOSE IT when a person brought it forward, which is the opposite
of what the mark is for.

## Answered from the surface, as the file requires

`frontSignal` answering from the surface rather than the engine is deliberate
and documented: `Agent.NeedsPerson` takes the agent's mutex and allocates a map,
the strip is laid out every frame, and over a remote handle the far side would
be a call per tab per frame. That is unchanged here.

The new reading is `asksStandingOrLanding`, one allocation-free walk over
`a.questions`, the same slice and the same shape as `asksHarness` and
`consentOpen` already use. No lock, no disk, no engine call.

## The exclusion is kept

An automatic proposal carrying a deadline is a countdown, not a question, and
`frontSignal` already excluded it. The new predicate names the two kinds it
counts rather than treating every question as a signal, so the countdown stays
out on both sides, and its doc comment says why.

## The test

`TestTheSameConversationAgreesInFrontAndBehind` puts the SAME conversation in
front and behind and compares the two answers. It carries its control in the
same test: a deadline proposal must also agree, and agree at `tabIdle`, so the
test would fail if the fix had widened the predicate into counting countdowns.

## The test that should have caught this and did not

`tabsignal_test.go` pins `tabNeedsPerson` for held tabs and for front tabs
separately, and `hopsignal_test.go` asserts the hop card and the tab signal
agree. None of them puts one conversation on both sides and compares, which is
the only shape that fails for this defect. This adds that shape.

## Checks

`go test ./internal/tui3`, the whole package, run four times over the work at
330.5s, 332.7s, 334.3s and 335.3s, on the base the work was written against
(`3d3b7542b`), plus focused runs of the new test. This branch is that work
cherry-picked onto the current head, so the gate's run here is the one that
counts.
